title: AutoParallel: Composable, PyTorch-Native Automatic Parallelism for Production Training
summary: Training large models requires multiple interacting forms of parallelism. As models and clusters scale, finding and maintaining efficient parallelization plans becomes essential for training performance. Diverse model architectures, workloads, and hardware topologies demand flexible strategies, yet production PyTorch systems typically rely on hand-written recipes that are costly to adapt and tend to reuse familiar patterns, which may be suboptimal for a given workload. We present AutoParallel, a PyTorch-native planner for distributed model training. AutoParallel searches parallelization choices jointly across the training computation, allowing established techniques to be combined and unconventional strategies to emerge. It expresses its decisions using native PyTorch abstractions and produces ordinary PyTorch programs, avoiding a separate execution runtime while composing directly with the PyTorch compilation and training stack. AutoParallel also composes automatic decisions with model-specific distributed code, allowing dynamic or specialized regions to remain under user control. Plans are inspectable and replayable artifacts. Across dense, hybrid, and mixture-of-experts models on meshes of up to four dimensions and 128 NVIDIA H100 GPUs, AutoParallel matches or exceeds expert-written TorchTitan recipes on most configurations, with throughput gains of up to 18.3%, and discovers plans that uniform expert recipes do not express.

title: CPU Micro-Architectural Characteristic Sensitivity Study on CPU-Side Agentic Task Latency
summary: We perform a novel study of CPU micro-architectural characteristics on how they affect agentic AI CPU side latency. Small enterprises and individual users looking to reduce costs and seeking data privacy benefit from running agents locally, motivating an investigation into the optimal performance characteristics of an edge CPU to improve user experience. We investigate the relationship between CPU core frequency, CPU uncore frequency, active physical cores, and symmetric multi threading with agentic task latency in single and multi agent configurations. Across eight experiments on an Intel edge CPU, we find that P-core frequency produces the largest median latency improvement among the evaluated parameters. Increasing P-core frequency from 2.5 to 5.5 GHz yields a 1.154$\times$ speedup for a single agent and a 1.341$\times$ speedup for eight concurrent agents. We are the first to characterize hardware micro-architectural relationships on single and multi agent configurations with TerminalBench; we also provide an open source framework and dataset for repeatable CPU side latency agentic benchmarking.

title: ResServe: Accurate and Efficient FP4 LLM Inference with Residue Compensation
comment: 26 pages, 20 figures, 9 tables, including appendices. Code: https://github.com/ShawRong/resserve
summary: Block-scaled 4-bit floating-point (FP4) quantization reduces large language model inference costs but can degrade task quality. Higher-precision computation can mitigate this loss at the expense of some of the efficiency gains from FP4 inference. Narrow matrix computations common in decoding often leave spare hardware capacity for low-cost precision recovery. ResServe combines an FP4 activation base with an FP4-quantized residue representing information lost during quantization. It uses this spare capacity to compute the residue's contribution and combines results on-chip, avoiding extra result transfers. We apply this principle to linear layers and decode attention, while selective compensation limits added work when processing input prompts. On NVIDIA B200, compensated linear kernels using the NVFP4 format improve numerical precision while retaining latency close to uncompensated execution for the evaluated operations with few rows. In the evaluated NVFP4 inference configurations, ResServe adds at most 3.4% request-latency overhead over W4A4 and reduces request latency by 22.4-53.3% relative to W4A8. Across five models, code-generation accuracy improves over same-format uncompensated inference, with mean relative gains of 15.04% for NVFP4 and 53.57% for MXFP4.

title: Measuring Bounded Autonomy for an LLM Decomposition Planner on a Live 5G-Core Testbed
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are entering network-management control loops, yet their plans can fall outside the executable action space. Whether hard deterministic bounds around such a planner have real effect, or merely restate a definition, is an empirical question. We measure it on a live 5G-core testbed, where an LLM planner decides when to decompose control-plane procedures into stateless handlers inside a bounded loop: a JSON schema constrains the output, a projection-repair validator re-checks it, a deterministic fallback guarantees liveness, and every decision is persisted. Three measurements anchor the paper. First, the two tested models, run unbounded with the allowed action sets stated in the prompt, still violated intent-handler rules in 13 of 44 standard calls. Every violation broke an intent-handler combination rule that the deployed flat schema cannot encode (schema enforcement as deployed caught 0/13); a union schema encoding the rule removes the class by construction. Second, with the bounds in place, all 33 decoded live plans were feasible without repair, and a matched-condition probe put the in-distribution unbounded rate at one violation in 20 windows. Third, exploratory: on the design set the planner matched an author-specified selection reference that a threshold policy and three a priori codings each missed. Transfer to held-out scenarios remained partial (5-6 of 10), and the planner's two-clause distillate could replace the runtime planner itself. Together, the results suggest elicitation and distillation, not runtime control, as the LLM's role.

title: RoadBlock: Rethinking GPU Tensor Core Microarchitecture for Emerging Microscaling Format Support
comment: Accepted to the ACM International Conference on Parallel Architectures and Compilation Techniques (PACT), 2026
summary: While multiple recent custom Microscaling (MX) format proposals preserve higher model quality over OCP MX, their hardware evaluations remain confined to standalone MAC-unit prototypes, ignoring the system-level integration overheads inside real GPU Tensor Cores. To this end, we present RoadBlock, an open-source framework for accurate end-to-end modeling of custom MX formats in a programmable Tensor Core, built on the RISC-V Vortex GPGPU. RoadBlock exposes data size, scale-factor size, and block size as configurable parameters and automatically derives per-thread metadata tiling for arbitrary formats, enabling format-specific Perplexity-PPA tradeoff evaluation before silicon commitment.

title: Stochastic AI Model Placement for AI-and-RAN Coexistence in 6G Networks
summary: This paper considers AI-service placement over geographically distributed RAN sites equipped with GPU resources partitioned into fixed, isolated multi-instance GPU (MIG) profiles. We propose C$^2$AIR, a chance-constrained optimization model that maximizes expected AI requests served while protecting uncertain RAN workloads and enforcing probabilistic capacity reliability requirements for admitted AI services. C$^2$AIR allows a service to run at multiple sites and accounts for discrete profile, memory, and GPU-slice constraints. We evaluate C$^2$AIR on a four-site deployment calibrated from NVIDIA Aerial RAN capacity figures and MLPerf Inference results, and on seven larger scenarios with up to 15 sites and 40 AI services, computing every violation and overload probability exactly from the demand distributions. C$^2$AIR keeps the RAN violation probability within its target at every hour of the day, whereas reserving for the mean RAN demand violates it in 24\% to 47\% of the intervals. The reliability condition prevents placing AI models that would be overloaded in 85\% of the intervals at an event hour, and multi-site replication serves 2.7 times more AI requests than single-site deployment. The evaluation also shows that coarse MIG instances and a heavy demand tail can make strict RAN protection expensive.

title: SAFTAC: Simulation-Augmented Fine-Tuning of Open-Source LLMs for Analog Circuit Design
summary: Circuit design for analog integrated circuits (ICs) is challenging because circuit topology, device sizing, and circuit performance are tightly coupled. Existing large language model (LLM)-based methods either rely on inference-time correction around frozen models or train on limited circuit types without directly using simulation outcomes as training signals. A key bottleneck is that existing datasets do not provide sufficient task information for training LLMs on end-to-end specification-conditioned design. To fill this gap, we first construct a large-scale simulation-grounded dataset with 8,626 design tasks across 10 different types of analog circuits, where each task includes a textual description, labeled I/O ports, loading condition, target specifications, a testbench, and a reference netlist. Using this dataset, we present SAFTAC, a simulation-augmented fine-tuning framework that trains LLMs to generate and revise analog circuit design. SAFTAC combines three-stage supervised fine-tuning, which progressively builds the capabilities required for analog circuit design and feedback-guided correction, with simulation feedback-augmented reinforcement fine-tuning, which further optimizes models using simulation-grounded rewards. We evaluate SAFTAC under single-pass generation and two-pass generation with simulation feedback, showing improvements over the strongest closed-source LLM by 15.9% and 7.8%, respectively.

title: Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline for Multi-Instance Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning
summary: We present the Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline (ASP), an offline rollout scheduler for multi-instance asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) of large language models (LLMs). ASP jointly reduces three sources of rollout underutilization - padding bubbles from intra-minibatch length heterogeneity, skewness bubbles from long-tail outputs, and sorting bubbles from fluctuations in training-queue occupancy induced by length-sorted dispatch - through a single offline preprocessing pass. This enables efficient multi-instance rollout that overcomes the early scaling plateau of single-instance inference while smoothing the arrival of generated samples at the trainer. We integrate the scheduler into an asynchronous architecture that decouples rollout from training while keeping policy lag observable and bounded. Complete ASP improves end-to-end throughput by up to 3.22 times and reduces iteration time by up to 76.8% relative to MindSpeed-RL, while reducing iteration time by up to 62.5% relative to verl. Within ASP, scheduling reduces mean iteration time by 10.9%. ASP also scales more robustly with additional generation resources than these baselines and shows no visible convergence degradation in the measured bounded-lag regime. ASP has since been used in an internal telecom-domain RL post-training workflow, reducing the reported training period from more than three months to about two months and producing a domain-enhanced model for knowledge answering and tool calling.

title: StarLoc: A Practical Approach to Encoding Geographic Locators in IPv6 for Starlink
summary: LEO satellite networks such as Starlink provide Internet connectivity across continents, oceans, and airspace. IP geolocation providers map Starlink's IPv6 prefixes to locations mainly through its self-published GeoFeed. However, users may be far away from their assigned Points of Presence (PoPs), one label covers an entire prefix, and labels and PoP mappings can change while addresses stay the same. We characterize Starlink's IPv6 addressing using 925 historical GeoFeed snapshots (2024--2026), one year of PoP mappings, and over 7.9 million observed IPv6 addresses. Our findings reveal that customer prefixes lack clear geographic structure, prefix labels lie a median of 540km from their PoPs, and relabeling a single /40 can affect the reported locations of up to 65,536 possible /56 delegations. To address these challenges, we propose StarLoc, a geographic Locator--Identifier separation scheme that embeds terminal location into IPv6 addresses using a resolution-adaptive H3 Locator while preserving existing Starlink prefixes, /56 delegations, and stable Endpoint Identifiers. To balance accuracy and privacy, StarLoc reveals only cells with at least a certain number of terminals, and operators can cap resolution in sensitive regions or withhold location entirely. Unlike topology-based schemes, StarLoc encodes physical location and lets Locators follow moving users.

title: Enabling Retraining-Free Accurate Inference in Analog Compute in Memory Accelerators
summary: Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) accelerators compute matrix-vector products directly inside memory arrays, eliminating weight movement and promising order-of-magnitude gains in inference efficiency. However, converter and device errors make pretrained models unusable on these arrays, and hardware-aware retraining is costly. We enable retraining-free, accurate inference of pretrained models on simple analog arrays with low-cost, shared calibration. Our key observation is that analog error depends on how each layer is represented on the array, and that this representation can be changed offline without changing the computation. We center the inputs and apply Hadamard rotations designed for analog arrays, which keep shared reference errors spread and confine input mixing to each array. Across CNNs, vision transformers and LLMs up to 14B parameters on PCM and ReRAM, the method brings vision models and larger LLMs within a few points of floating-point accuracy and matches or approaches published hardware-aware training without training any weights. On ReRAM with 6-bit ADCs, it restores ViT-B/16 from 37.4% to 82.9% and Phi-4 from 27.0% to 72.2%, both within 2.2 points of floating-point accuracy.

title: Age of Information for Power-Saving Devices with DRX Mechanism
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Published in IEEE ICC 2023
summary: Reducing the power consumption of User Equipment (UE) has always been a crucial issue in communication systems. As a result, Discontinuous reception (DRX) is introduced in today's New Radio (NR) networks as a power-saving strategy. In addition, the variety of low latency applications in 6G makes the issue of maintaining data freshness increasingly important. This paper aims to study the relationship between freshness and power-saving. To capture the information freshness, we use Age of Information (AoI) as the performance metric. To our best knowledge, unlike previous studies focusing on power saving and delay trade-offs, this is the first study considering the impact of DRX on AoI. We solve the closed-form solution of the peak average AoI with the DRX mechanism. Moreover, we propose a parameters adjustment strategy. Based on the simulation validation, our proposed strategy can enable the UE to keep the AoI close to the theoretical lower bound AoI while achieving high power-saving efficiency.

title: TwinHash: Two-Sided Object Identity Management for Time- and Energy-Efficient Agentic Workflows
summary: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) services interleave large language model (LLM) generation with external tool execution, and increasingly rely on search-based workflows that repeatedly revisit shared reasoning states and computations. These patterns create substantial redundancy across tool outputs, LLM responses, and key-value (KV) prefixes, yet existing serving systems primarily optimize shared prompt prefixes, while naive input-keyed caching is unsafe when identical requests produce different outputs. We present TwinHash, a unified object management architecture that assigns each object an input-side hash key to recognize repeated requests and an output-side content fingerprint to validate and locate stored state, complemented by type-specific reuse guards that preserve correctness and response diversity. A software object identity table maintains reusable objects across requests and trajectories, while a hardware object placement table tracks their residency across hierarchical memory tiers so that evicted state can be retrieved rather than recomputed. Across seven agent frameworks and five benchmark suites, reuse follows workflow structure more than benchmark identity. TwinHash serves up to 81% of tool outputs wherever deterministic tool reads recur, and up to 92% of LLM responses in search-based frameworks. Retrieving an evicted KV-prefix from DRAM reduces TTFT by up to 5.6x on Qwen3-32B, with greater gains projected for larger dense models. Under search-based frameworks, TwinHash reduces end-to-end wall-clock time by up to 87% and measured task energy by up to 81% over a prefix-cached baseline, while a per-key serving cap controls the quality-reuse trade-off in adaptive search. These results demonstrate that unified identity, safety, and placement management can convert structural redundancy in emerging agentic workflows into substantial serving-efficiency gains.

title: More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow
summary: Translating parallel scientific codes between HPC programming frameworks is a critical but labor-intensive task. Existing LLM-based approaches rely on fixed sequential pipelines with undifferentiated repair strategies and correctness criteria that do not match scientific computing practice. We present an agent-skill framework that separates translation, compilation diagnosis, and execution validation into three autonomous agents coordinated by a verdict-driven orchestrator, routing each failure to a targeted repair skill rather than retrying blindly. An automated output check drives the self-correction loop, complemented by an offline LLM-based verification that exposes false positives escaping compiler and runtime checks. We evaluate the framework on 30 HeCBench kernels translated bidirectionally among CUDA, OpenMP, and SYCL with three open-source LLMs. Our framework attains the higher verified correctness rate in all 18 model and direction combinations over a state-of-the-art baseline while consuming up to 52.4% fewer tokens, remaining consistent across models and directions without architectural modification.

title: Adaptive Age of Information Optimization in Rateless Coding-Based Multicast-Enabled Sensor Networks
comment: 20 pages, 11 figures, 3 tables. Published in IEEE Journal of Selected Areas in Sensors, 2024
summary: As the demand for real-time information in Internet of Things (IoT) and Wireless Sensor Networks (WSN) scenarios grows with the evolution of bandwidth-intensive 5G applications, multicast transmission becomes increasingly vital. This paper delves into the significant role of multicast in WSN, exploring a novel perspective of using rateless codes over the traditionally employed Hybrid automatic repeat request (HARQ) for eliminating retransmissions in a wireless multicast system. We aim to optimize data freshness, quantified by the Age of Information (AoI), and analyze strategies to minimize time-average AoI in a multicast environment with diverse channel conditions. Specifically, our policy focuses on optimizing the time-average AoI based on sensor devices' feedback. We transform the problem into a Markov Decision Process (MDP) to locate optimal and low-complexity suboptimal policies. We present the first age-minimum scheme for rateless code-based wireless multicast systems. Our numerical simulations reveal that the proposed policies, developed considering unique system structural properties, consistently surpass baseline strategies. We are thus able to preempt updates at the most beneficial time, thereby addressing the issue of the bottleneck device's adverse impact on overall performance.

title: Memory as a Temporal Resource: Lifetime Contracts for Multi-Retention Systems
summary: Computers move and rewrite data whose useful lifetimes range from inner-loop iterations to years, yet memory systems usually hide retention as a fixed physical property. We argue that required lifetime should become a first-class resource across algorithms, programming systems, controllers, and devices. Building on prior lifetime-aware placement, we propose an event-based validity contract that links application completion events to retention-class selection and renewal of protection. Applications would be enabled to express semantic contracts such as ``until this tile completes'' and the system will map data to homogeneous arrays engineered for ephemeral, epoch, or durable retention and preserve correctness through margins, ECC, refresh, migration, or recomputation. We present a trace-based simulator and FPGA prototype that exercises class migration.

title: Capital Efficiency, Isolation, Risk, and Ruin in Generative AI Inference Serving Infrastructure
summary: Generative AI serving is an extremely capital-intensive endeavor that demands rapid, step-change improvements in capital efficiency to prevent industry wide increases in the cost of capital from limiting growth plans. Keeping pace with the economic necessities will increasingly require infrastructure providers to confront operationally-inconvenient realities of production serving, including the extreme heterogeneity of generative AI request costs. We have explored workload isolation as a foundational, fleet-level lever for increasing capital efficiency. Isolation is the practice of intelligently grouping "like" requests before execution. Rather than exposing every replica to the full heterogeneous workload distribution, isolation deliberately reshapes the workload presented to the hardware by assigning requests with different cost characteristics to different portions of the fleet. Workload isolation on its own does not make expensive requests cheaper; it prevents a costly portion of the workload from unnecessarily determining the operating point and capital efficiency of the entire fleet. It additionally lays the foundational groundwork that can serve as a launching point for compounding gains via narrow-band optimizations (tailoring) and custom silicon designs while also informing up on pricing policy. This paper uses representative production data and experience to convey the motivation behind isolation as a fleet-level lever for increased capital efficiency.

title: Computation-Efficient Aerial-Marine Integrated Networks for Search and Rescue via Cooperative HAPS, UAVs, and MASSs
summary: In this paper, we propose an aerial-marine integrated network architecture tailored for maritime search and rescue (MSAR) operations, where a high altitude platform station (HAPS) and maritime autonomous surface ships (MASSs) are equipped with edge servers, providing computing services for surveillance uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs). These UAVs generate substantial volumes of computation-intensive and delay sensitive tasks, some of which can be strategically offloaded to both MASSs and HAPSs for distributed processing. We formulate the joint task offloading and resource allocation as a mixed-integer nonlinear program (MINLP) to minimize the system computation overhead (CO), quantified by a weighted sum of task completion time and energy consumption. Given the stochastic nature of task arrivals from UAVs and the dynamic characteristics of marine channel conditions, we employ a two-stage optimization to decompose the problem into four tractable subproblems, i.e., 1) edge server selection, 2) transmission power allocation, 3) edge computing resource allocation, and 4) local computation resource allocation. In stage I, we optimize the edge server selection via many-to-one matching. In stage II, we determine the transmission power of each UAV with quasi-convex optimization and solve the edge computing and local computing resource allocation subproblems via a projected gradient descent method and convex optimization, respectively. Simulation results validate that the proposed scheme can achieve superior system performance over benchmark schemes.

title: ISER-MoE: Dynamic In-Switch Replication of Hot Experts for Load Balancing in Expert-Parallel
summary: Expert-parallel mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers run at the pace of the most loaded GPU, and a few hot experts carry most of the excess load. Replicating them at every MoE layer balances the load only if their weights arrive within the layer, and broadcasting from the owner is the bottleneck: point-to-point copies overload it, and baseline broadcasts pay latency or bandwidth overheads. We present ISER-MoE (In-Switch Expert Replication for MoE), built in TensorRT-LLM, which multicasts hot experts through the NVLink switch to fixed GPU groups, so each byte leaves its owner once. A GPU scheduler assigns hot experts to groups per layer, and a multi-port broadcast spreads the injection over the group's ports, both overlapped with the shared expert. In trace replay, the scheduler removed 98-99% of the excess load; in prefill serving of DeepSeek-V4-Pro, throughput rose 17.4% on a math benchmark and 7.2% on agentic prompts.

title: An Empirical Evaluation of a Weighted PALU Model for Internet Traffic Networks
summary: The PALU model is a hybrid power law generative framework that decomposes Internet traffic graphs into three structural components: a preferential attachment core, degree one leaf nodes, and disconnected satellite clusters. Although the original PALU formulation provided a theoretical basis for this decomposition, it was never validated against real traffic data and was restricted to unweighted networks. This work presents the first empirical evaluation of PALU against real Internet traffic, using packet traces from the MAWI WIDE samplepoint F dataset. We introduce a weighted extension of the model incorporating strength degree scaling, and develop a packet-to-graph pipeline for parameter estimation across multiple observation window sizes. Results show that the power law degree exponent $α\approx 2.0$ remains stable across observation scales from $10^5$ to $3 \times 10^6$ packets, consistent with the PALU structural prediction. However, the satellite cluster parameter $λ$ and the weighted scaling parameter $θ$ exhibit systematic dependence on observation scale, and the Poisson star assumption for unattached components is formally rejected at all tested window sizes. These results indicate that PALU captures important aspects of Internet traffic structure but requires an explicit observation model to fully account for finite sampling effects.

title: Scalable Full-Horizon SFC Deployment over Predictable SAGIN Topologies via Configurable Column Generation Framework
summary: Space-air-ground integrated networks (SAGINs) integrate heterogeneous communication and computing resources to support ubiquitous services. Service function chains (SFCs) enable complex services to be composed of ordered functions and executed collaboratively across these resources. Mobility continuously reshapes connectivity throughout service execution, yet much of the resulting topology evolution is predictable. Decisions based only on isolated topology snapshots may therefore overlook valuable future connectivity. We formulate an admission-first, cost-aware model on a time-expanded graph for SFC deployment. Our key observation is that temporal feasibility is request-specific, whereas global coupling arises mainly from shared-resource competition. We therefore develop a configurable column-generation framework in which complete request deployments form columns and a restricted master problem coordinates admission and resources. SAGINFE, a fast constructive heuristic built on per-flow embedding (PFE), supplies a standalone feasible solution and initial columns. Configurable pricing schedules combine early-terminated and stricter searches, supplemented by selective PFE candidates. Candidates undergo feasibility and exact reduced-cost checks. Request-wise pricing can run in parallel, followed by finite-pool integer selection. The default configuration improves the admission-first objective over initialization on all 120 main instances. Four pricing workers achieve up to a 2.69-fold median pricing-stage speedup while preserving admitted request counts in the tested cases.

title: DARIC: A Position-Independent KV Cache Reuse System with Distribution-Aware Recomputation
summary: The context lengths of large language models (LLMs) are rapidly increasing in real-world applications such as agentic systems and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). To accelerate LLM inference in these scenarios, reusing position-independent key-value (KV) caches across requests has emerged as a promising approach. This technique typically relies on recomputing a selected subset of tokens to restore cross-chunk interactions. However, existing solutions suffer from critical limitations in both algorithmic efficiency and system deployment. Algorithmically, they overlook the distribution of KV cache deviations, leading to either high token-selection overhead or degraded generation quality. At the system level, the reliance on custom LLM execution flows for recomputation complicates deployment and prevents seamless integration with highly optimized inference engines. In this paper, we propose DARIC (\textbf{D}istribution-\textbf{A}ware \textbf{R}ecomputation for \textbf{I}ndependent KV \textbf{C}ache Reuse), a novel KV cache reuse method based on system-algorithm co-design. At its core, DARIC introduces a distribution-aware token selection strategy that adaptively schedules token recomputation based on empirical KV deviation patterns, striking an optimal balance between generation quality and computational efficiency. Moreover, DARIC is built on a lightweight system architecture that enables independent KV cache generation and recomputation with minimal integration overhead, fully preserving existing system-level optimizations of standard inference engines. Comprehensive experiments across various datasets and LLMs demonstrate that DARIC consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 1.1$\times$--4.5$\times$ speedup in time-to-first-token (TTFT) with negligible loss in generation quality. Code is available at https://github.com/Lenovo-ICI/DARIC.

title: 5G-NetBotSim: A Synchronized Co-Simulation Framework for Connected Robots over ROS and srsRAN-based 5G Network
summary: Connected robotic applications increasingly rely on wireless communication for teleoperation, coordination, and distributed autonomy. However, robotic simulators often use ideal links or abstract delay models that do not capture cellular scheduling and protocol processing effects. We present 5G NetBotSim, a realtime co simulation framework integrating ROS/Gazebo workloads with an executable, full stack srsRAN 5G network emulator. The framework provides isolated User Equipment (UE) robot contexts and stage level timing across the host, gNB, UE, ROS, and robot execution stages. We evaluate human to robot teleoperation and robot to robot leader follower coordination under controlled channel quality conditions. Results show how CQI and MCS variations propagate to throughput, communication latency, and robot performance. In leader follower coordination, higher channel quality reduces mean tracking error from 0.558 m to 0.460 m, a 17.6% reduction. These results demonstrate protocol stack in the loop co simulation for joint network and robotic-application evaluation.

title: UniExit: A Unified Latency-Aware Early-Exit Runtime for Heterogeneous Edge AI
comment: 15 pages, 20 figures. Accepted to ACM SenSys 2027 (The International Conference on Embedded Artificial Intelligence and Sensing Systems)
summary: Edge applications increasingly combine CNN-based perception with edge-deployable Transformer-based language models, but deploying such heterogeneous workloads on resource-constrained devices is challenging because inference latency varies with both input difficulty and runtime hardware state. Early-exit inference reduces computation by terminating at intermediate stages, yet existing methods are often model-specific and rely on static latency profiles that become stale under dynamic edge conditions. This paper presents UniExit, a unified latency-aware early-exit runtime for heterogeneous edge AI. UniExit abstracts CNN blocks and Transformer layers as ordered stages and applies a common latency-aware routing policy while retaining model-specific quality mechanisms. It predicts the cost of reaching the next exit from runtime state and inference progress to make budget-aware continue-or-exit decisions. UniExit combines runtime-state-aware latency prediction, cache-based prediction reuse, trend-aware fallback, and CNN-specific exit stabilization to provide low-overhead and robust online control. We implement UniExit on multiple edge and edge-cloud platforms and evaluate it with representative CNN and Transformer-based language-model workloads. Across single-workload, concurrent heterogeneous, and edge-cloud settings, UniExit consistently improves deadline satisfaction and latency-accuracy trade-offs over existing progressive inference baselines, while reducing redundant exit-module computation and task-level energy consumption.

title: Link-Level Performance Comparison of 5G Beamforming: Reciprocity-Based SVD vs. Codebook-Based Precoding
comment: 7 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to IEEE ICC 2027
summary: Downlink (DL) precoding in mid-band MIMO relies on uplink (UL) sounding reference signals (SRS) with reciprocity-based singular value decomposition (SVD) or channel state information reference signals (CSI-RS) with codebook-based precoding matrix indicator (PMI) feedback. Although SVD precoding offers unquantized beamforming, it depends on a channel estimate from SRS transmitted at the limited user equipment (UE) power, whereas Type-I PMI is quantized but derived from a high-power CSI-RS based channel estimate. In this paper, we compare SRS-SVD and CSIRS-PMI for single-user MIMO through an end-to-end, 3GPP-compliant link-level simulation at 3.75 GHz with 100 MHz bandwidth, using a 192 antenna element gNB mapped into 32 ports, the 3GPP Release 19 UE antenna model, and ray-traced (RT) channels in Manhattan and Chicago. We show that neither scheme is uniformly superior: CSIRS-PMI serves weak and shadowed users better and reduces outage, whereas SRS-SVD achieves higher spectral efficiency (SE) and enables more multi-layer transmission for users with strong channels. The results on the Clustered Delay Line (CDL)-C statistical channel also confirm this crossover. We further show that by utilizing a simple logistic regression based on the received power of the standard CSI reference signal (CSI-RSRP) and the channel quality indicator (CQI), the gNB can select the optimal transmission scheme with around 90% accuracy, achieving an SE that closely approaches an ideal per-user selection.

title: RPEG: Training Reasoning Language Models Scalably and Cost-Effectively
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is now central to training Reasoning Language Models (RLMs), but RLM pipelines are difficult to scale and costly to run because each RL step couples multiple large models, heterogeneous stages, cross-step state, and complex asynchronous dependencies. Existing systems typically optimize only parts of this design space. We address this complexity by jointly optimizing the pipeline structure as well as its execution using a novel data-centric graph intermediate representation called RLM Pipeline Execution Graph (RPEG). RPEG exposes structural choices such as bounded asynchrony and actor-critic sharing together with execution optimizations such as stage fusion, fine-grained scheduling, and multi-dimensional model parallelism. It is coupled with a comprehensive analytical performance model for RLM training, jointly capturing compute, communication, memory, and hierarchical rack-, node-, and GPU-level effects. Across systems with up to 256 GH200 GPUs, our distributed runtime engine implementing RPEG improves performance by up to 2x over ReaL and reduces step latency by up to 2.48x over verl, while increasing hardware utilization by up to 30%. Overall, RPEG provides a graph-driven foundation for next-generation training pipelines for frontier reasoning LLMs.

title: Green500: Adventure in Qualifying a Cluster
summary: Energy effciency has become a key metric for evaluating High Performance Computing (HPC) systems, as reflected by the Green500 ranking. However, energy effciency alone does not capture the full environmental impact of an HPC cluster. Using the Kuma cluster at EPFL, we report on two Green500 measurement campaigns at Level 2 and Level 3, and extend this analysis to a full carbon footprint assessment using the MITSI life-cycle based methodology. GPU power capping experiments show that energy effciency peaks at 450 W, achieving an 11% performance loss offset by a 20% reduction in energy consumption. When embodied emissions are accounted for, the optimal power cap for carbon effciency shifts to 500 W under Switzerland's low-carbon electrical grid, revealing a tension between minimizing usage and embodied contributions. We discuss the challenges of generalizing this approach into a broader carbon-based HPC ranking, and argue that moving beyond energy effciency is both necessary and feasible.

title: DataHelix: A CPU-GPU Co-Scheduling Data Plane for Multimodal Model Training
summary: Multimodal model training breaks the loose coupling between data loading and model execution assumed by conventional training pipelines. Large per-sample variation in decoding cost, token/latent count, and tensor size causes both CPU preprocessing time and GPU compute time to vary substantially across data-parallel ranks (training processes). In synchronous training, these two sources of heterogeneity interact tightly: GPU execution determines how long the input pipeline has to prepare the next batch, while delayed preprocessing in any rank in turn stalls all GPUs at synchronization. As a result, optimizing CPU throughput or GPU load balance in isolation cannot eliminate pipeline bubbles. We present DataHelix, a metadata-first CPU-GPU co-scheduling data plane for multimodal training. DataHelix jointly reasons about preprocessing demand and GPU execution progress, treating each GPU compute window as the readiness budget for the next batch and coordinating preprocessing across ranks to minimize deadline misses rather than CPU makespan. To avoid expensive data movement, placement is decided while samples remain lightweight descriptors, before decoding and collation amplify them into large tensors. Descriptor-level token-latent-aware batching performs coarse pre-balancing, while cost-gated collective rebalancing corrects residual skew only when its expected benefit exceeds transfer cost. Across 11 video and multimodal workloads on 8 Ascend 910B accelerators, DataHelix reduces mean deadline-miss rate by 67.8% and mean p95 input-wait latency by 87.0%, while achieving 2.72x geometric-mean throughput over rank-local DataLoaders and 1.82x over a Ray actor pool under the same CPU budget.

title: Nebula: Distributed Position-Independent Caching for LLM Serving
summary:
Modern LLM workflows, such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and LLM agents, build long prompts from multiple independent text segments, making prefill a major source of computation. Reusing KV caches is therefore important for reducing serving costs and latency: distributed caching systems spread KV cache across a cluster to increase aggregate capacity, while position-independent caching (PIC) enables reuse of recurring segments under different prefixes. However, existing systems distribute KV caches but still rely on prefix caching (PC), while existing PIC methods enable position-independent reuse without cluster-wide resource management.
  We present Nebula, the first distributed LLM serving framework to treat PIC segments as first-class citizens, enabling remote PIC reuse and parallel prefill. To track PIC's fine-grained, asynchronous state changes, Nebula combines optimistic accounting with event-driven updates to provide a timely and truthful cluster view for cache management and prefill scheduling. To accommodate diverse reuse patterns across workloads, Nebula leverages cluster-wide ghost-hit feedback to automatically tune the allocation of shared cache capacity between PC and PIC. Finally, Nebula incorporates queueing, computation, and KV transfer costs into a unified prefill completion time model to guide elastic parallelism adjustment and locality-aware compute placement. Across four models and four real-world RAG and agentic workloads, Nebula reduces median TTFT by an average of 61.4% compared with the strongest existing baseline and recovers an average of 76.1% of the tokens missed by prefix caching.

title: Towards Sustainable Federated Learning via Carbon-Aware Client Selection
summary: The Information/Communication Technology (ICT) industry is severely challenging the global environment due to the sharply rising carbon emissions generated by machine learning (ML) workloads. Federated Learning (FL) is one of the prominent distributed ML systems used in applications with billions of client devices, such as Google Gboard and Apple Siri. Nearly half of the total carbon footprint in FL originates from client-side computation during local training. However, existing client selection strategies in FL primarily focus on minimizing energy consumption rather than carbon emissions, despite the fact that carbon impact depends not only on computational load but also on the underlying carbon intensity of the energy source. In this paper, we address this gap by proposing a carbon-aware fair client selection strategy (CA-FCS) designed to minimize the carbon emissions associated with model training on client devices. In contrast to existing approaches for reducing carbon emissions in FL, we incorporate hourly carbon intensity and a realistic energy consumption model developed using empirical measurements from Google Pixel smartphones to estimate client-side carbon emissions in FL. Since repeatedly selecting low-carbon clients may reduce data diversity and degrade global model performance, particularly under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data settings, CA-FCS incorporates fairness into client selection to mitigate this issue. We conduct extensive experiments under realistic FL settings for mobile devices, where client participation is constrained by device availability conditions, such as charging status and Wi-Fi connectivity. The results demonstrate that our method reduces client-side carbon emissions by up to 46% while maintaining competitive model accuracy.

title: Fast and Actionable Classification of HPC I/O Time Series
summary: Input/output (I/O) is a major bottleneck for highperformance computing (HPC) performance. One of the challenges is the contention between jobs when sharing the parallel file system. However, tackling this issue depends on knowing the temporal behavior of jobs. In this paper, we propose a clusteringbased approach to characterize jobs' temporal I/O behavior. We propose SAGE, a lightweight method that cuts I/O traces into short windows and learns an alphabet from them. The trace then becomes a sequence of symbols, which we call ''genome'', and we use clustering to separate them into classes. We evaluate SAGE and its two-stage variant SAGE-2 on 819,771 real traces from 2 HPC systems. We compare them against other techniques from the state of the art on three metrics, including one we propose. Compared to K-shape, the best baseline available, SAGE-2 lowers the median intra-cluster metrics by 9.1% on average, and achieves this in 2 minutes of clustering time versus 3.8 hours, a 109x speedup. More importantly, clusters created by SAGE and SAGE-2 carry enough information to act on: we evaluate the use of the cluster centroids for I/O scheduling, and show that our approach can decrease I/O stretch by up to 24% compared to the state of the art (round-robin placement).

title: Concurrent Use of FP32 and FP64 Computing Units on GPUs and Mixed-Precision Placement in WENO Reconstruction
summary: Scientific computing often requires FP64 arithmetic, although FP64 performance is limited on NVIDIA GPUs. Double-float (DF) emulation, which represents a value using two FP32 values with about 48 bits of significand, outperforms native FP64 where FP64 units are limited. On the other hand, mixed-precision strategies offload to FP32 the operations that do not determine accuracy. In both approaches, the native FP64 units remain idle during FP32 instruction execution. We investigated whether this idle resource can be recovered on A100, GH200, GB200, and RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q. A microbenchmark shows that co-resident FP32 and native-FP64 kernels exceed the throughput of the faster kernel alone on A100 but not on GH200 and GB200; on RTX 6000 Blackwell, they do so against FFMA but, against DF emulation, only when the issue density of the DF kernel is reduced. We then tested whether this gain carries over to computing the WENO-Z reconstruction with the nonlinear weights in FP32 and the candidate polynomials in native FP64 (W32P64). We observe substantial overlap on A100, whereas GH200, GB200, and RTX 6000 Blackwell show little overlap. Importantly, the fastest placement does not always preserve the design accuracy of WENO-Z: for a one-dimensional entropy wave problem, W32P64 fails to achieve the design order of accuracy for WENO7 and WENO9. In contrast, DF emulation of the entire reconstruction comes close to it on the grids tested for WENO5, WENO7, and WENO9 while delivering a $2.51-3.94 \times$ speedup over FP64 on RTX 6000 Blackwell. For WENO5 on the two-dimensional Euler vortex problem the W32P64 error at $n=256$ is $1.26 \times$ that of FP64 and 1/104 of that of the all-FP32 reconstruction.
